transcript.content:
Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-01-20 11:57 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-01-20T10:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 59.542 degrees and its azimuth is 151.107 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 47.814 degrees and its azimuth is 124.404 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 2.74 percent illuminated, 19.022 degrees from the Sun, and 385267.8 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest: **No, you will not be able to see it.**

Even though your app correctly shows that the Moon is physically "above the horizon," there are three specific reasons why it will be invisible to the naked eye in these conditions:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Effect
The Sun is at an altitude of nearly 60 degrees. At that angle, the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight (Rayleigh scattering). This creates a high level of "sky brightness." Because the Moon is only 2.74% illuminated, it is essentially a very thin, dark sliver. The ambient light of a clear day in Lagos is far too intense for the human eye to distinguish a faint, sliver-thin crescent against the blue of the sky.

### 2. The Proximity to the Sun (Elongation)
The Moon is only 19 degrees away from the Sun. In astronomy, this is a very small elongation. Because the Moon is so close to the Sun in the sky, it is sitting in the brightest part of the atmosphere. Even if the Moon were a Full Moon, it would be difficult to see at that proximity; since it is a tiny crescent, it is effectively "lost" in the glare.

### 3. Contrast Ratios
Human vision relies on contrast. To see the Moon during the day, it usually needs to be near Full or Gibbous, where its reflected surface is bright enough to compete with the scattered blue light of the atmosphere. A 2.74% crescent has almost no surface area reflecting light toward you. It is functionally the same as trying to see a dark grey needle against a bright white background.

**The Verdict:**
If you look toward the azimuth of 124° (South-East), you will see a very bright, clear sky. You might see some high-altitude clouds or haze, but the Moon will be completely invisible to your unaided eyes. It is "there," but it is being drowned out by the Sun's overwhelming radiance.
